name: Enets, Forest
confidence_why: Tereshchenko 1993, repeated in Siegl 2013, puts word stress predominantly on the first syllable, and Khanina 2018 agrees the first syllable is the prominent one more often than not but finds no clearly fixed stress, with the second syllable also often prominent, so the initial placement is secure while the strictness of the rule is not.
catalog_citation: Siegl 2013: Materials on Forest Enets, an Indigenous Language of Northern Siberia (MSFOu 267)
catalog_locator: sec. 2.11 'Stress', p. 102, (footnote callouts 148, 149 omitted from the quote)
catalog_quote: Stress is fixed and the main stress falls on the first syllable; therefore it does not need to be marked separately. Stress is realized in terms of intensity, and vowels in stressed syllables tend to be slightly longer than unstressed ones. A weak secondary stress falls on the following odd-numbered syllables. ... Tereščenko (1966: 441) listed some native lexemes, which she reported as having stress on non-initial syllables, however none turned out to be stressed in this position in contemporary Forest Enets. ... A random test with several consultants showed that such lexemes are nevertheless stressed initially.
readall_conflicts: The one listed work (Siegl 2011, open copy) is silent, so nothing here contradicts the catalog's StressTyp2 initial-stress record. However, three Enets works already held by the project in the same check folder from the 2026-09-16 pass (not in this task's works list) hedge the 'fixed initial' reading and should be weighed when the site entry is. Khanina 2018 ( lines 191-205, printed p. 433, sec. 1.4, on Enets = Forest and Tundra together): 'As is typical for Uralic languages, the first syllable is often more prominent in Enets than other syllables: all three stress-related parameters (length, intensity, and pitch) can contribute to prominence. The second syllable can also be prominent; further syllables are rarely prominent, though there are some exceptions connected to some affixes that tend to be prominent.. In short, the situation with Enets stress is very messy and a proper study of stress in Enets is yet to be undertaken. For the moment, it is only clear that there is no easily identifiable fixed stress in Enets, and that the first syllable is more prominent than other syllables more often than not.' Khanina & Shluinsky 2022 (the text layeroffprint p. 5, sec. 2.2): 'Phonetic realization of stress does not display any distinctions in the two Enets either.' Pleshak 2022 (the text layerand 331-333, printed pp. 285-286) reports Tereshchenko 1966: 441 as claiming 'that in addition to the first syllable, other odd syllables get stressed in Enets' and 'every odd syllable in an…

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (initial), not in the strict set; keep rule 10/100/1000.. as the dominant pattern, keep Siegl's odd-syllable secondary stress in the primary-stress rule, add caution citing Khanina 2018:433 ('no easily identifiable fixed stress.. first syllable is more prominent.. more often than not; second syllable can also be prominent') and Tereshchenko 1993:345 'преимущественно' / 1966:441 'чаще всего' with her non-initial minimal pairs. Rationale: of four primary statements held, only Siegl 2013 says 'fixed'; the two Tereshchenko sketches hedge and the newest phonology article denies fixedness while agreeing initial is dominant. If the compilers prefers to keep fixed-strict on Siegl's consultant re-test, the minimum action is a caution/contra entry for Khanina 2018.

No instrumental word-stress study was found. (4) Hence the initial location is we

sources.citation: Pleshak, Polina. 2022. On Enets intonation patterns of Enets-Russian bilinguals. In: Hämeenmaalta Jamalille. Kirja Tapani Salmiselle, pp. 279ff. Helsinki. hdl 10138/342430
sources.quote: Second-hand on word stress: 'there has been almost no work done on Enets prosody so far'; cites Khanina (2018:433) that 'the most prominent syllable is the first one' and 'there is no lexical stress in Enets that would be easily identifiable', and Tereshchenko (1966:441) that 'every odd syllable in an Enets word is prominent'; characterises Enets word-level prosody as 'based on the rhythm, rather than logical prominence'. Pilot phrasal-intonation study, not a word-stress study.
